Scope of what I can assert: with pretrained knowledge only, and no access to the SCOPe parseable files (dir.des, dir.cla, dir.hie) or the release history pages, I can describe the classification issue that PDB 1acc raises and the methodological consequences, but I cannot certify the exact sunids, sids, residue boundaries, or the specific release in which any renumbering took effect. Those are release-specific facts that must be read off the files for the two releases being compared, and I flag them as unverified below rather than inventing them.

The entity: 1acc is the 1997 crystal structure of the protective antigen component of Bacillus anthracis (the PA83 protein, widely studied as the antigen in anthrax vaccines). Its single long chain A (roughly 735 ordered residues) was described in the original structure paper as four distinct structural domains. For a structural classification this is the hard case: one chain, one SEQRES, four compact units with different folds and different evolutionary histories.

What changed between SCOP 1.75 and newer SCOPe releases: SCOP 1.75 (the 2009 final SCOP release, which remains the frozen reference set used by ASTRAL 1.75, SCOP-based benchmarks, and most published remote-homology datasets) carried domain definitions for 1acc chain A that were coarser and partly protein-specific: the chain's units were grouped under protective-antigen-specific fold/superfamily/family lineages rather than being linked to the wider families that each module belongs to. In the SCOPe 2.0x series (Fox, Brenner and Chandonia's continuation at Berkeley), curators revisited entries of this kind. The relevant kind of change for 1acc chain A is (a) adjustment of the domain boundaries and the number of domains carved out of the chain, so the sid suffixes shift (a whole-chain or three-way split becoming a four-way split means d1acca1 through d1acca4 no longer denote the same residue spans as before), and (b) reassignment of at least one unit out of a toxin-specific lineage into a lineage shared with non-toxin proteins. The best-established example of (b) for this protein is the N-terminal module, which is the namesake of the PA14 domain: that module was later recognised in beta-glucosidases and other glycoside hydrolases, in fungal adhesins of the Epa/Flo type, in some bacterial proteases, and in various carbohydrate-binding proteins. Treating the N-terminal unit as a member of a widely distributed module, rather than as a piece of a toxin-only fold, is the substantive classification change. I want to be explicit that I am not able to confirm from memory which SCOPe release number implemented each step, nor the exact post-change sids and ranges; verify against SCOPe's release notes and the dir.cla/dir.des entries for 1acc before citing specifics.

What this reveals about domains as evolutionary modules: three things. First, the evolutionary unit is the domain, not the chain and not the protein's biological role. A single gene product here concatenates modules with independent phylogenetic distributions; one of them is shared with enzymes and adhesins that have nothing to do with this protein's biology. Domain shuffling and recombination, not whole-chain descent, generated this architecture. Second, domain boundaries are hypotheses, not measurements. They were revised because new structures and new sequence coverage made a different parse more defensible, which means a boundary is only as stable as the evidence available when it was drawn. Third, the hierarchy levels carry different evidential weight and the revision is mostly a statement about which level applies. Membership in the same family asserts clear common ancestry, usually with detectable sequence similarity or very strong structural and functional evidence. Superfamily asserts probable common ancestry inferred from structure plus weaker functional or structural signals, with sequence identity often below the detectable range. Fold asserts only that the major secondary structures are in the same arrangement and topology, and explicitly does not assert homology: fold-level neighbours can be convergent or simply the result of a limited repertoire of favourable packings. Moving a unit from a protein-specific family into a module-level superfamily is an upgrade in inferred evolutionary breadth; it is not a claim that the toxin and a glucosidase do the same thing.

Unsafe transfers to avoid, stated explicitly. (1) Do not transfer function along the shared module. The PA14-type module's recurrence in binding proteins and enzymes does not let you infer anything about this protein's role, nor the reverse; shared modules are often repurposed, and in this protein the module sits in a completely different architectural and functional context. Function transfer is only defensible at family level with corroborating experimental evidence, and even then catalytic residues and ligand sites must be checked individually. (2) Do not transfer homology claims across a fold boundary. If two units are only fold-level neighbours in SCOPe, they are not evidence of common ancestry and must not be reported as homologues. (3) Do not treat an interface, an oligomeric assembly, or a biological unit as a domain. SCOPe domains are structural and evolutionary units; a functional site built from several domains or several chains has no single SCOPe label. (4) Do not carry SCOP 1.75 sids forward as if they were stable identifiers. A sid like d1acca1 is a slot in one release's parse; after a reparse the same string can denote different residues. Identifiers must always be read together with their release version and their residue range, and cross-release work should match on ranges, not on strings.

How this should affect homology searches. Search and score per domain, not per chain. A full-length 1acc chain A query will produce a composite profile in which the signal from any one module is diluted; split the chain into its SCOPe domains (or into independently predicted units) and run each separately, then reconcile. Expect multi-domain hits to be partial: a genuine PA14-module hit to a glucosidase will cover only a few hundred residues of the query and should be judged on the aligned region's statistics and coverage, not on a global score, and HHsearch, HMMER or Foldseek outputs should be read with per-domain coverage in view. Treat any hit found through a module that the query shares with distant proteins as an architecture-level relationship only, and annotate it as such. For benchmarking, do not mix releases: a method trained or evaluated on ASTRAL/SCOP 1.75 splits and tested against SCOPe 2.0x labels will see boundary and lineage changes as apparent errors, and reported accuracy differences can be artefacts of curation rather than of the method; fix one release per experiment and state it. For structure prediction and template-based modelling, select templates per domain as well; a template chosen on whole-chain similarity may be correct for one module and wrong for the rest, and in this protein the modules differ enough that a single template for the whole chain is not defensible. Finally, since representative selection in ASTRAL depends on the domain parse, the representative set changes when the parse changes: a sequence-identity-filtered set built on an older parse can silently retain near-duplicate modules or drop a module entirely, so rebuild representative sets from the release you are actually using.

Required external evidence before relying on any of the above specifics: the dir.des, dir.cla and dir.hie files for SCOP 1.75 and for the target SCOPe release, to recover the actual sunids, sids and residue ranges on both sides; the SCOPe release notes and change history for 1acc, to date the change; the PDB entry and its SIFTS mapping, to reconcile author numbering with SEQRES and UniProt coordinates; and Pfam/InterPro records for the PA14 module, to confirm its distribution independently of SCOPe. Sequence-level corroboration (profile-profile or HMM searches) should accompany any superfamily-level homology claim, and experimental evidence should accompany any function claim.
